title: Quantum Interconnects Part I: Strategic Quantum Network Formation
abstract: The realization of large-scale quantum networks requires more than advances in quantum repeaters, memories, and processors, it requires a framework explaining how heterogeneous quantum technologies evolve from isolated deployments into interconnected infrastructures. While the classical Internet evolved under strong utility incentives associated with resource sharing and communication demands, quantum networking currently lacks dominant applications capable of generating comparable incentives. As a consequence, contemporary quantum networks are largely formed through technology-driven decisions motivated by technical feasibility, experimental validation, and expected future value. This work argues that the absence of utility-driven network formation is not solely a consequence of immature applications, but also of insufficient abstraction. In particular, heterogeneous quantum platforms remain tightly coupled to the functionalities they provide, preventing the definition of technology-independent utility functions. A hierarchical architecture consisting of Physical Platforms (PP), Functionalities (F), Services (S), Applications (A), and Use-Cases (UC) is proposed, together with the argument that quantum interconnects constitute the enabling technology required to decouple physical implementations from network functionalities. Such decoupling permits the definition of utility functions at the functionality level and establishes the conditions under which strategic (agent-based) network formation becomes applicable. Quantum interconnects should therefore be viewed not only as interoperability devices, but also as fundamental enablers of strategic quantum network evolution.
summary: This paper addresses the gap in understanding how heterogeneous quantum technologies can form large-scale networks. It proposes a five-level hierarchical model to abstract physical platforms into reusable functionalities. The central argument is that quantum interconnects are crucial enablers that allow this abstraction, thereby enabling the definition of utility functions necessary for strategic, market-like network growth.
main_problem: The challenge is developing a framework to explain the evolution of large-scale quantum networks from isolated, heterogeneous technologies into interconnected infrastructures driven by utility rather than mere technical feasibility.
main_result: The authors propose a hierarchical architecture (PP $ightarrow$ F $ightarrow$ S $ightarrow$ A $ightarrow$ UC) and argue that quantum interconnects are fundamental enablers that allow for the necessary abstraction to define utility functions and enable strategic, agent-based network formation.
method: The work uses a conceptual modeling approach, proposing a hierarchical abstraction framework and modifying network formation models (like agent-based models) to incorporate utility derived from functional interoperability.
model_or_system: The model describes heterogeneous quantum platforms (e.g., quantum dots, trapped ions) connected by quantum interconnects. The system is conceptualized through a five-level hierarchy: Physical Platforms, Functionalities, Services, Applications, and Use-Cases.
key_observables: Utility functions ($U_i$), interoperability parameters ($I_{ij}$), and the degree of abstraction achieved at the functionality level.
important_parameters: The structure of the utility function, which must be defined independently of the underlying physical platform.
main_assumptions: The core assumption is that quantum interconnects provide sufficient interoperability to decouple network functionalities from specific physical implementations, thereby enabling utility-driven decision-making.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the transition from a technology-driven strategic landscape to an expected utility-driven landscape, supported by the proposed hierarchical model.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the problem (technology-driven growth), proposes the hierarchical abstraction framework (PP to UC), develops the role of interconnects in enabling functional decoupling, and concludes by showing how this enables utility-based, agent-driven network formation.
why_interesting: It provides a high-level theoretical framework for understanding the necessary architectural evolution of quantum networks, framing interconnects not just as physical links but as abstract enablers of utility.
